essence: Adelma is a harbour where every face the traveller meets resembles someone he knew who has died, until he suspects that he has arrived there dying himself and that the afterlife is a crowded port without joy.
textDetails: The narrator had never travelled as far as Adelma before; he lands there at dusk.
On the dock, the sailor who catches the mooring rope and ties it to a bollard looks like a man who had served as a soldier with the narrator and who is dead.
It is the hour of the wholesale fish market.
An old man is loading a basket of sea urchins onto a cart; he resembles a fisherman who was already old in the narrator's childhood, and when the narrator turns back he has disappeared down an alley.
A fever victim lies huddled on the ground, a blanket over his head; the narrator's father, days before his death, had the same yellow eyes and stubbly beard.
The narrator averts his eyes and stops daring to look anyone in the face.

He weighs two possibilities: if Adelma is a dream city where only the dead are met, the dream frightens him; if it is a real city of living people, looking longer would dissolve the likenesses into strangers' faces full of anguish; either way he had better not stare.
In the vegetable market a vendor weighs a cabbage on a scale and drops it into a basket that a girl lets down on a string from a balcony.
The girl is the image of a girl from his village who went mad for love and killed herself; the vendor lifts her face and she is his grandmother.

He reflects that there comes a time when, among the people you have known, the dead outnumber the living, and the mind, refusing new faces and expressions, stamps the old forms on every new face, choosing the best-fitting mask for each.
Stevedores file up the steps, bent under demijohns and barrels, faces hidden by sackcloth hoods; impatient and afraid, he waits for them to straighten up so he can recognise them.
In the narrow, crammed streets unexpected faces resurface from far away and stare at him as if asking to be recognised, as if recognising him, as if they already had.
He wonders whether to each of them he too resembles someone dead; barely arrived, he has already crossed over to their side, absorbed into a kaleidoscope of eyes, wrinkles and grimaces.
He concludes that Adelma may be the city where one arrives dying and meets again the people one knew, which means he too is dead, and that the hereafter is not a happy place.
Note: apart from the yellow eyes the text names no colours, lamps or season; the sea and the ship are implied by the landing, the dock, the rope and the fish market rather than described.
visualConcept: A steep harbour town climbs a dark hill out of an endless still sea at dusk, its houses packed so tightly that the alleys are slots of shadow. Along the quay stand iron bollards, a moored coastal ship, an arcaded wholesale fish market heaped with silver fish and black sea urchins, and a small vegetable market under a balcony; up the middle of the town runs one long straight flight of steps on which a line of hooded stevedores toils under demijohns and barrels. Hundreds of tiny townspeople crowd every quay, stall and stair, and each has a small face-disc that stays dark and anonymous until the traveller looks at it. The traveller, a cloaked figure with a lantern who steps off the ship, casts a soft visible cone of gaze; every face it touches flushes into a pale bone-white mask, the face of someone he has lost, and turns to stare after him. Within a minute the hillside is a field of small moon-pale faces all turned toward one man, the dead outnumbering the living, until the porters straighten and his own face goes white too. The base is the sea itself: the town is a rock island with no edge but the water, fading into blue-grey sea mist.
layout: Footprint: a crescent hill-island, radius about 20 at the waterline, its straight south edge facing the sea, rising in five terraces (each about 1.8 higher) to y 9 at the back. Fish market: an open loggia of 7 arches (10 long, 2.5 deep, 2.8 tall, tiled roof) on the west half of the quay, with crates of silver fish (instanced ellipsoids), baskets of sea urchins (violet-black spheres with short spines) and the old man's two-wheeled cart; the blanketed fever victim against its east end wall. Town: about 170 tall narrow houses (1.0-1.8 wide, 2.5-6 tall) on the terraces, alleys 0.5-0.8 wide, about 40 percent of the tiny windows lit, a bell tower (9 tall) at the top as a landmark. signatureMotion: 1) Arrival at dusk, an 80 s loop: the ship slides out of the sea mist with its stern lantern lit; the sailor on the quay catches the thrown rope and loops it round a bollard; the traveller steps ashore and walks a fixed route past the fish market and the fever victim, up to the vegetable market (the basket descends on its string, the cabbage is weighed, the basket rises) and on to the foot of the steps. 2) Masks of the dead: the traveller's gaze is a soft additive cone (35 degrees, 7 units long) that sweeps left and right as he walks; any face it touches blooms into a bone-white mask over 0.6 s, carrying a faint procedural pattern of eye-hollows and wrinkles that slowly reshuffles like a kaleidoscope, and the figure turns to face him and keeps tracking him. The scripted encounters get their own beats: the sailor first; the old man, who fades away down an alley once recognised; the fever victim, whose mask is tinged sallow yellow; the girl on the balcony; and the vendor, who lifts her face as the basket rises. By the time he reaches the steps about 90 percent of the faces glow. 3) The turn: the line of stevedores halts and stays bent for a long beat, then straightens one by one as the hoods fall back to show glowing masks; at that instant the traveller's own face whitens, his lantern gutters out and he steps sideways into the crowd. The masks dim slowly as the light sinks, then the dusk resets and the next ship's lantern appears in the mist.
interactionDescription: Reverses the direction of recognition. Off: the traveller's lantern-gaze prints the masks of his dead onto strangers. On: the gaze cone disappears and every face in the town turns to him at once; hundreds of fine silver sight-lines run from their masks to his face in a converging web; his own face whitens into a mask like theirs and his lantern dims. The camera rises up the stair to the arch and looks down at him from among the crowd, so the viewer stands with the dead, regarding a newcomer who resembles someone they lost.
mood: Dusk just after sunset. A narrow copper band lies on the sea horizon under a slate-blue sky going to night; the water darkens to deep teal and holds the last light in long streaks; a low mist drifts off the sea into the alleys; wet stone glints; a few warm window lights and the ship's lantern are the only warmth. The faces glow cool bone-white like a crowd of small moons. Hushed, feverish, melancholy.
caption: You land in Adelma at dusk, while the fish market is in full cry, and the sailor who makes your rope fast has the face of a comrade long dead. An old man loading sea urchins, a woman weighing cabbages, porters hooded under their barrels: each is someone you have lost. Look longer and the crowd looks back, as if it knew you too. Perhaps this is where the dying come ashore, and the shore is not glad.
motto: When your dead outnumber your living, every stranger arrives masked.
camera: From the sea just south of the quay: distance 36 from target (0, 4, -4), elevation 14 degrees, field of view 38.
